Entries.Text: Save every modified effect to every binder that holds it, including a value still being typed.
Save every modified effect to every binder that holds it.
Drop the selected effect's unsaved changes and read it again from the project's files. This clears the undo history.
Every effect in the project's sfx binders. An effect stored in several binders is edited once and saved to all of them.
No effects were found in the project's sfx folder.

Toggle the display of effect names from the Particles alias list. Current Mode:
{0}

Switch between one flat list of effects and effects grouped by the binder file they come from. An effect stored in several binders is listed under each, and saves to all of them.
Current Mode: {0}
Copy the effect ID to the clipboard.
Drop this effect's unsaved changes and read it again from the project's files. This clears the undo history.
The effect's states and node tree. Each node runs the config its state chooses; configs list the states that use them.
The selected item. Values are shown in fxr-main's units (seconds, degrees); the raw view shows what the file stores.
Select an action in the Effect Tree to see its values.
When a condition is true, the effect moves to its target state (or ends).
The action's name, type and slot, from the FXR schema.
Show the words and properties exactly as the file stores them.
Show values whose purpose isn't known yet (named unk_ in the schema).
The FXR schema has no layout for this action in {0}, so only its raw values are shown.
This action stores more values than the schema describes, so only its raw values are shown.
Greyed names aren't stored in the file and use the schema default; editing one adds it.
Values whose purpose isn't known yet.
Shown in display units (e.g. seconds or degrees); the file stores a different unit.
Not stored in the file: the schema default is shown.
Go to {0} in the FX Editor
Opens the FX Editor with this effect selected. Ctrl+click the value does the same.
{0}: no sfx binder holds this effect
An id (88300) or a file name (s88300, s88300_a, s88300_a.tpf, s88300.flver). The file stores the id; the slot decides which texture type is loaded. 0 is none.
Not an id or a resource name: it is dropped when you leave the field.
The action's fields as stored (index, hex, int, float) and its properties.

Plays the selected effect in the viewport. PointSprite, BillboardEx and MultiTextureBillboardEx particles are drawn with their textures, colours and sizes; Tracer trails and Line/QuadLine particles as strips; Model particles with their FLVER; PointLight and SpotLight particles as lights. Distortion, radial blur, lens flares and GPU particles come later. The wireframes show each node's origin and emitter shape in the preview state, at time 0. The selected node's shapes are yellow.
Draw PointSprite, BillboardEx and MultiTextureBillboardEx particles as textured quads, with their blend modes. A texture that is still loading, or that no binder holds, draws as a soft round spot.
Scales the colour of every billboard. Effect colours are over-bright (HDR) values, and how the game maps them to the screen isn't known exactly, so this lets you match the look of the game.
The brightness multiplier. 1x draws the colours as stored.
{0} trail and line segments, {1} models, {2} of {3} lights.

In the game an effect usually moves: it flies with a projectile or swings with a weapon. Trails, equal-distance emitters and detached particles depend on that motion, so the preview can move the effect the same way.
Still: the effect stays at the origin. Forward: it flies along +Z, as a projectile. Swing: it moves round a circle, as a weapon's tip in a slash. Changing this replays the effect.
How fast the effect flies forward.
The radius of the circle the effect moves round, about the Y axis.
How fast the effect goes round the circle.
Move the camera with the effect, so it stays in view. The wireframes stay where the effect started.

Scales the intensity of the effect's lights. Light intensities vary a lot between games (DS3's are around 0.1, AC6's around 50), and how they map to the viewport's lights isn't known, so this lets you match the game.
The light intensity multiplier. 1x uses diffuseMultiplier × the colour's alpha as stored.
Draw Model and RichModel particles with their FLVER (sfx model s<id>), lit like other models. Their colour, UV scrolling and animation aren't applied yet. At most 200 per appearance.
Add PointLight and SpotLight particles to the viewport as lights. They light the models in the viewport. The viewport draws 15 at most, the brightest ones.
Mark each light with a cross and a ring at its range, and a spot light with its direction.
No binder holds these textures, so they draw as soft spots: {0} ({1} in all).
The running effect: the state it is in, and how many particles and nodes it has. Its state changes by its own conditions, which read the time and the external values below.
Select an effect to run it.
Terminated: emitters have stopped, and what is left plays out.
Finished: nothing of the effect is left. Restart to play it again.
The preview's limit of {0} particles or {1} nodes was reached, so some weren't made.
A Proxy node starts an effect that isn't in the project, so it shows nothing.
End the effect, as reaching state -1 does: each node then follows its Termination action. Restarting, scrubbing back or an edit plays it again from the start without this.
Draw each live particle as a small white cross, on top of its billboard: useful to see particles that are too small, too faint or hidden. At most 20000 are drawn.
Start, pause and restart the effect's clock, and frame the effect in the viewport.
Start or pause the effect's clock.
Start the effect again from time 0.
Move the camera so the whole effect is in view.
The effect's time since it started, in seconds.
Drag to move to a time. This pauses playback.
How long the effect plays before it loops or stops. Effects have no stored length: they end by their state conditions, so this is set by hand.
Start the effect again when the playback length is reached. Otherwise playback stops there.
How fast the effect's clock runs compared with real time.
The playback speed. 1x is real time.
The effect state the wireframes show. Each node uses the config its StateConfigMap gives this state.
The state index, from 0 to the effect's last state.
Values the game sets on a running effect. State conditions and some properties read them, for example Terminate (0) ending an effect. Ids not listed read as 0.
The value the effect reads for this id.
Remove this value. It then reads as 0.
The id of an external value to add.
Add the external value with this id.
What the viewport draws for the selected effect.
Draw each emitter's shape (point, disk, rectangle, sphere, box or cylinder) at its node, with an orange arrow for the particles' initial direction where it has one.
Draw each node's origin as short red (X), green (Y) and blue (Z) lines. Proxy nodes are marked with a magenta cross.
Click to edit this curve in the Curve Editor.
The property picked in the Action Inspector: how its value changes over time, its keys and its modifiers. Changes are one undo step each, made once you let go of a value or a dragged key.
Click a property's name in the Action Inspector to edit it here.
The selected value isn't a property of this action.
The action and property being edited, and what drives it.
the node's active time when the particle was emitted
nothing: the value at time 0 is used
How the value is stored: a constant, or keys joined in steps, straight lines or curves.
Changing the function keeps the keys where it can. Tangents start flat when changing between Bezier and Hermite, as they mean different things.
Each key's value holds until the next key.
Smooth curves between the keys, shaped by each key's slopes.
Eased curves between the keys, shaped by two angles stored on the key before each segment. The graph uses fxr-main's approximation of the game's curve.
A Hermite curve per component, each with keys of its own (AC6 and Nightreign).
Repeat the curve after its last key. A looping curve with all its keys at 0 has no length, which the game reads as an invalid value.
The length a Component Hermite curve stores. It grows to cover the last key.
The value over time, in the inspector's units. Shaded bands show the range the random modifiers spread it over.
Drag a key to move it in time and value; the yellow keys are the selected component's. Double-click to add a key there. Scroll to zoom, right-drag to pan.
The keys in time order. Keys are put back in order when an edit is committed.
The constant value. Turn it into keys with the Function above.
Component Hermite keeps keys per component; this picks which component's keys are listed and dragged.
The key's time, in seconds of what drives the property.
The key's value, one per component.
The slope as the curve leaves this key, in value per second.
The slope as the curve arrives at this key, in value per second.
The tangent angles of the segment after this key, in radians as stored (0 to about 1.57). They aren't converted like the values.
Remove this key. A curve keeps at least one key.
Add a key after the last one, with the curve's value there.
Changes made to the property's value: random variation per instance, or scaling by an external value. Ranges are shown in the inspector's units.
Add a modifier. It starts with no effect: a range of 0, or a factor of 1.
A random value between the base minus the delta and the base plus the delta, per particle or node.
Adds a random value between the minimum and the maximum, per particle or node.
A random value up to the fraction away from the base value (0.5: between half and one and a half times it).
Multiplies the value by a factor that depends on an external value the game sets, like the time of day.
As External Value 1, but read only when the effect starts (Elden Ring uses it for blood visibility, AC6 for external value 2000).
One value per component, in the inspector's units (a fraction isn't converted).
The seed the random value is picked with, per component. Particles with the same seeds vary together.
The id of the external value the factor is read by (0 Terminate, 1 precipitation, 2 time of day, ...).
A key of the factor curve: the external value, then the factor for each component.
